candidates.name: Racket define-match-expander
candidates.reason: A named compile-time transformer can expand a grammar-level abbreviation into a full match pattern, centralizing repeated structure while preserving readable match arms.
candidates.application_scope: Transferable language design for reusable pattern-position abstractions within an existing matcher.
candidates.constraints_or_caveat: Requires adaptation to Rust's binding, type and exhaustiveness rules; it is not an importable Rust library.
candidates.date_evidence: The opened official archive dates Racket 6.0 to February 2014, and its opened version-specific reference specifies define-match-expander. The separately opened current 9.3 manual is later evidence, not the basis of this date.

candidates.name: GHC pattern synonyms
candidates.reason: Parameterized pattern synonyms give repeated nested destructuring a grammar-oriented name without forcing a change to the underlying data representation.
candidates.application_scope: Transferable pattern-abstraction mechanism for matching AST or token structures.
candidates.constraints_or_caveat: A Rust counterpart needs binding, type and exhaustiveness semantics; the precise 7.8.1 feature set was not checked because its release notes could not be decoded.
candidates.date_evidence: The opened official manual explicitly identifies PatternSynonyms as available since GHC 7.8.1; the opened official 7.8.1 release page dates that version to 2014-04-09. This supports availability of the core mechanism before cutoff; the live 9.14.1 manual itself remains post-decision evidence.
candidates.historical_detail_verification: Incomplete: the linked 7.8.1 release notes failed to decode.

candidates.name: LALRPOP grammar macros
candidates.reason: Parameterized grammar macros factor recurring productions into named reusable forms while generating a Rust parser from a grammar that can be compared with the specification.
candidates.application_scope: Alternative parser architecture when repetition reflects grammar productions or token sequences.
candidates.constraints_or_caveat: Requires adopting a generator grammar and build workflow; does not itself provide a reusable fragment inside an existing Rust match pattern.
candidates.date_evidence: Only the undated live repository README was verified; no dated version establishing availability by 2014-05-27 was opened.

candidates.name: rust-peg parameterized grammar rules
candidates.reason: Named grammar rules with arguments provide reusable parsing templates inside a compact Rust grammar macro, allowing recurring recognition structure to follow specification terminology.
candidates.application_scope: Alternative for parser portions expressible as reusable grammar productions.
candidates.constraints_or_caveat: Moves reuse into a PEG grammar rather than native Rust patterns; grammar semantics and error behavior must be checked when translating an existing parser.
candidates.date_evidence: The opened live README verifies parameterized rule templates but supplies no dated historical version supporting availability before cutoff.

candidates.name: combine parser combinators
candidates.reason: Reusable parser values and combinators can replace repeated recognition logic with named grammar components assembled through ordinary Rust expressions.
candidates.application_scope: Parser refactoring when the repeated match code recognizes input sequences rather than only destructuring a value.
candidates.constraints_or_caveat: Does not add pattern-position syntax; its default LL(1) behavior and opt-in lookahead require checking against the existing parser's recognition behavior.

raw_response:
Five catalogue-sourced options are useful for this problem. Racket and GHC supply direct precedents for naming reusable pattern structure. The three Rust libraries offer broader parser refactorings when the repeated matches correspond to grammar productions.

1. Racket define-match-expander
   Source: https://download.racket-lang.org/releases/6.0/doc/reference/match.html
   Discovery catalogue: https://github.com/avelino/awesome-racket
   A named compile-time transformer can expand a grammar-level abbreviation into a full match pattern, centralizing repeated structure while preserving readable match arms. This is a design precedent for a Rust pattern abstraction, with Rust-specific binding, typing and exhaustiveness work still required. The archived 6.0 manual verifies the mechanism, and the official archive dates that release to February 2014: https://download.racket-lang.org/all-versions.html

2. GHC pattern synonyms
   Source: https://downloads.haskell.org/ghc/latest/docs/users_guide/exts/pattern_synonyms.html
   Discovery catalogue: https://github.com/krispo/awesome-haskell
   Parameterized pattern synonyms give repeated nested destructuring a grammar-oriented name without forcing a change to the underlying data representation. They are a transferable language mechanism, not a Rust component. The current official manual says the extension began with 7.8.1, and the official release page dates 7.8.1 to 2014-04-09: https://www.haskell.org/ghc/download_ghc_7_8_1.html. Its historical release notes failed to decode, so the exact old feature set remains incompletely checked.

3. LALRPOP grammar macros
   Source: https://github.com/lalrpop/lalrpop
   Discovery catalogue: https://github.com/awesome-rust-com/awesome-rust
   Parameterized grammar macros factor recurring productions into named reusable forms while generating a Rust parser from a grammar that can be compared with the specification. This fits repetition at the production level, including recurring lists or production subsets. It requires a parser-generator workflow and is not a local abbreviation inside an existing Rust match pattern. Historical availability is unknown because only the live README was verified.

4. rust-peg parameterized grammar rules
   Source: https://github.com/kevinmehall/rust-peg
   Discovery catalogue: https://github.com/awesome-rust-com/awesome-rust
   Named grammar rules with arguments provide reusable parsing templates inside a compact Rust grammar macro, allowing recurring recognition structure to follow specification terminology. This may help if rewriting the relevant parser portions as grammar rules is acceptable. It does not supply native match-pattern aliases, and grammar semantics and error behavior need checking during translation. Historical availability is unknown from the opened live README.

5. combine parser combinators
   Source: https://github.com/Marwes/combine
   Discovery catalogue: https://github.com/awesome-rust-com/awesome-rust
   Reusable parser values and combinators can replace repeated recognition logic with named grammar components assembled through ordinary Rust expressions. This is useful when the match expressions implement input recognition; it is less direct for repeated destructuring alone. The default LL(1) behavior and explicit lookahead choices must fit the existing parser. Historical availability is unknown from the opened live README.

The applicability judgments above are translation by an internal model, not measured deployment outcomes. Racket has an opened archived manual before the cutoff. GHC's core mechanism has a historical availability statement plus a dated release, while its opened descriptive manual is later evidence. The Rust-library evidence is undated and must not be treated as proof of availability by 2014-05-27.
